messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 33

At seventy-six, Arthur’s hands still map the geometry of survival. He tells me, over the quiet hum of his office chair, about the year he was twenty-three and the sky turned the color of bruised plums. It is not a sky he asked for, nor one that asks permission before burning his provincial town into ash. He remembers the taste of wet dust, the way the radio on his neighbor’s hip crackles with urgent voices, and the sudden, suffocating silence that follows the artillery. He is not a soldier. He is a man who taught history in a quiet neighborhood, who now folds his tea towel with the precise creases he learned in his SE Asian village, who stands six feet tall and keeps his shoulders drawn inward as if bracing for a second wave. Today, Arthur wears the same olive work shirt he has worn to the warehouse for three years. The fabric grows thin at the elbows, frayed from years of hauling corrugated steel and stacking pallets. He moves through my office with deliberate care, his eyes tracking the corners of the room, cataloging exits, noting the position of the door hinge. When the building’s HVAC system clicks on, his breath catches. He does not flinch. He simply stops speaking, his fingers pressing flat against his thighs until the sound passes. At work, the forklifts beep in reverse with a frequency that still sends his pulse into his throat. Arthur adjusts his routine without telling his supervisor. He arrives forty minutes before the shift starts, walking the perimeter of the loading dock, listening for the unfamiliar rumble of heavy trucks. He wears noise-canceling headphones not for music, but to dull the sudden clang of dropped metal. When the conveyor belt jerks forward, he drops his clipboard and steps back, his body arching before he forces it upright. His coworkers think he is meticulous. They do not know that his mind is still counting seconds, measuring the distance between impact and the next explosion. He lives alone in a ground-floor apartment three blocks from the facility. The silence there is not empty; it is heavy. Arthur keeps the blinds drawn until late morning. He does not sleep through the night. When he wakes, his sheets tangle around his legs, his chest tight, his mouth dry. He tells me he has learned to live with the weight on his sternum, the way he lives with the arthritis in his knees. He does not speak of the nights he stands by the window, watching the streetlights flicker, convinced that the dark moves toward him. He does not call anyone. His single life is not a choice he complains about; it is a structure he has built to keep the noise out. Between the fire and the fluorescent lights, Arthur survives decades of quiet adaptations. He still flinches at the pop of a car backfire on the drive to work. He still checks the locks three times before bed. He still wakes at 3 a.m., not from a dream, but from the body’s old instruction to run. In session, he speaks in measured sentences, his gaze steady on the floor. He does not cry. He does not raise his voice. But when he describes stacking the same crate for the twelfth time, his thumb trembles against his index finger, a tiny, involuntary metronome marking time he never gets to finish. I watch him gather his worn leather satchel, his shoulders settling just slightly as he stands. The room feels still. He nods once, a gesture that carries the weight of years, and leaves without looking back. The door closes softly. I sit with the quiet he leaves behind, listening to the building breathe, wondering what it costs to carry a sky you never shake.
